## Quarto

Quarto enables you to weave together content and executable code into a finished document. To learn more about Quarto see <https://quarto.org>.

## Running Code

When you click the **Render** button a document will be generated that includes both content and the output of embedded code. You can embed code like this:

```{r}
1 + 1
```

You can add options to executable code like this

```{r}
#| echo: true
2 * 2
```

The `echo: false` option disables the printing of code (only output is displayed).

Question:

➡️ Create one document for two of the most common formats: HTML and Word. Render ![](data:image/png;base64,) each of the three documents.

- How does the output differ?

  Answer:

  Html : render output as .html file. the output can interact with web. html also enables interactive features like interactive data visualization.

  word : renders .docx file which can only open and edit on desktop. word output are static images

- Looking at the YAML at the top of the document, how does the input differ?

  Answer:The input between the two is different int in format. for html we get "format:html " and for word we get "format: docx".

## **Markdown**

Markdown is a lightweight set of conventions for formatting plain text files.

### **Headings**

Headings and subheadings can be included in a file to organize the document. make sure to leave a space between the \# and heading.

#1st Level Header

##2nd Level Header

###3rd Level Header

## Including R code chunks

R code chunks in R are include by pressing "Option+ Command + i"

### **Links and Images**

Hyperlinks and external images or GIFs can be included in Quarto documents as well.

### Hyperlinks

\[linked phrase\](<http://example.com>+) "if i remove the + sign, the link name will be shown as below."

### **Text Formatting**

Basic formatting of text, such as italicizing, bolding, superscripts, and subscripts can be implemented as well.

| Raw text input   | Rendered output |
|------------------|-----------------|
| \*italic\*       | *italic*        |
| \*\*bold\*\*     | **bold**        |
| \`code\`         | code            |
| superscript\^2\^ | superscript2    |
| subscript\~2\~   | subscript2      |

## **Code Chunks**

adding **code chunks** to the file, allows us to run R code inside our document:

There are several ways to insert a code chunk:

1.  The keyboard shortcut Cmd/Ctrl + Alt + I (recommended)

2.  The “Insert” button icon in the editor toolbar (top right).

3.  By manually typing the chunk delimiters

Activity_5:

➡️ Add a new code chunk at the bottom of the Quarto document, naming the chunk uptown-chunk by including **#\| label: uptown-chunk** as the first line inside the code chunk.

Solution:

```{r}
#| label: uptown-chunk

scores <- c(3,5,2,8)
mean(scores)

```

Activity_6:

➡️ In the code chunk, use the include_graphics() function from the knitr package to include the image at the following URL:<https://github.com/dilernia/STA418-518/blob/main/uptownFunk2.png?raw=true>. Note that the URL should be enclosed in quotes when calling the include_graphics() function.

solution:

```{r}
#| label: uptown-chunk2

### Use of knitr::include_graphics()
knitr::include_graphics("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dilernia/STA418-518/refs/heads/main/uptownFunk2.png") 
```

**Why use `knitr::include_graphics()`?**

- **Consistency:**It handles pathing seamlessly across different output formats (like HTML, PDF, and Word).
- **Quarto Integration:**It allows you to use chunk options like #\| out.width: "80%"`or`#\| fig.align: "center"\`to control how the image looks in your final document.

solution:

note:during the output, the code will be hidden and only image will output set by #\| echo: false


### Chunk Option Behaviour

| `eval` | `include` | Does code execute? | Is code shown in report? | Are results/images shown? | Common Use Case |
|----|----|:--:|:--:|:--:|----|
| **`true`** | **`true`** | Yes | Depends on `echo` | Yes | Standard active chunk for plots/text/images. |
| **`true`** | **`false`** | Yes | No | No | Quiet data setup, loading libraries/scripts. |
| **`false`** | **`true`** | No | Depends on `echo` | No | Displaying example code without running it. |
| **`false`** | **`false`** | No | No | No | Deactivating/omitting chunk from document. |

### Customizing the YAML (at the top of the Quarto document) 

-–\
title: “Document title”\
author: “Author name”\
date: today\
format:\
html:\
self-contained: true\
embed-resources: true\
execute:\
eval: true \# Evaluate code\
echo: true \# Show code\
warning: false \# Suppress warnings\
message: false \# Suppress messages\
-–

### Including plots

first, nstall.packages(‘tidyverse’) to the Console if not installed.

excercise: plotting a scatter plot on storms ⛈️ between 1975 and 2021 from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) data.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
# Load storms data set
data(storms)

storms |> ggplot(aes(x = pressure, y = wind)) +
  geom_point()

```

### Inline Code

```{r}
xbar<-2
se<-1.3
```

The 95% confidence interval for the mean is (`r xbar - 1.96 * se`, `r xbar + 1.96 * se`)

Activity 10.

➡️ Include a chunk of R code and after that in-line R code at the bottom of the document to reproduce the sentence containing the confidence interval results above.

solution:

A.chunk R code

```{r}
xbar<-4
se<-2.3
confidence_interval<- c( (xbar - 1.96 * se), (xbar - 1.96 * se) )
confidence_interval
```

B. In-line code

The 95% confidence interval for the mean is (`r xbar - 1.96 * se`, `r xbar + 1.96 * se`)

### Tables

Continueing with the storms data set looking at the four largest sustained wind speeds recorded for different storms.

```{r}
#Largest sustained wind speeds recorded
storms_summary<- storms |>
  group_by(name, year) |>
  summarize(max_wind_knots =max(wind)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  slice_max(max_wind_knots, n=4)

library(knitr)
storms_summary |>
  kable()
```

#### ***kable() from the knitr package***

The kable() function includes tables in Quarto documents for PDF, HTML, and Word outputs.

### customizing table captions

```{r}
#| label: ‘tbl-a_table_name #label option must begin with "tbl" prefix

#| tbl-cap: ‘A custom table caption’
```

#### ***flextable() from the flextable package***

flextable() function from flextable package displays tables for all output formats in a more consistent manner, with a large number of methods for customization that work for all output formats as shown @tbl-storms

```{r}
#| label: tbl-storms
#| tbl-cap: "Table made with kable()"
library(flextable)

storms_summary |>
  flextable() |>
  colformat_double(big.mark="", digits=0) |>
  autofit()

  
```

### get() from the gt package

get() function from get package has a wide range of formatting options, including conditional formatting and group-wise summary statistics. It is most easily used with HTML as the output format for Quarto, but not as easily for PDF or Word output when further customizing the table.

```{r}
library(gt)

storms_summary |>
  gt()
```

### Table Themes

customizing aspects about tables displayed in Quarto using flextable () function.

```{r}
# Displaying flextable with tron theme
#| label: storms_summary
storms_summary |>
  flextable() |>
  autofit() |>
  theme_tron()

```

Activity 11:

➡️ Display the storms_summary table applying a complete theme different than the one used above using the flextable() function by viewing the available themes here:

solution:

```{r}
#| label: flextable-zebra-theme
library(flextable)
# Displaying flextable with a clean zebra theme
storms_summary |>
```

Activity 12.

➡️ Display the storms_summary table applying a complete theme different than the one used above using the gt() function and the [gtExtras](https://jthomasmock.github.io/gtExtras/reference/index.html) R package by viewing the available themes here: <https://jthomasmock.github.io/gtExtras/reference/index.html>

```{r}
library(gt)
library(gtExtras)

# Combine everything into a single, connected pipeline
storms_summary |>
  gt(id = "tbl-custom") |> 
  gt_theme_dot_matrix()
```
